title: What is known about 1RB1LC_0LC---_1RE1LD_1RD0LA_1RF0RC_0RA1RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_0LC---_1RE1LD_1RD0LA_1RF0RC_0RA1RC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. At every moment the visited part grows on the right, the tape is (10)^x 1^4 (01)^n1 1^3 (01)^n2 1^3 … (01)^nk 1 0 1, and between two such moments the j-th counter from the right loses exactly 2j, for the counters up to some point from the right; beyond it the list is rebuilt. This is measured, not proved. Halting needs A on a 0 with a 1 to its right, which never happens in the first 109 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 80,023 cells have been visited and 40,016 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 5.93×10<sup>18</sup> steps (exact macro run)
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 6 cells, long runs of equal blocks crossed in one go; exact: every macro step is a run of the machine, counted step for step) ran from blank tape to step 5,931,313,351,842,280,547 without a halt. At this block size it gives the same state, head position and tape as the direct simulator after 2,000,038,489 steps. This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.511). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.15).

claims.title: Shift rules of the sweeps
claims.text: Lean proves, for every count and every tape around, the four shift rules by which the sweeps cross the blocks: C crosses (10)^n leftward and (01)^n rightward (turning it into (10)^n), A crosses (01)^n leftward, E crosses (10)^n rightward (turning it into (01)^n).

claims.title: The tape is a list of counters
claims.text: Each time the visited part grows on the right (in A, then B), the tape is (10)^x 1^4 (01)^n1 1^3 (01)^n2 1^3 … 1^3 (01)^nk 1 0 1 B>0, e.g. at step 233,350,399: x = 2461 and the counters 2693 3139 1283 339 5487 1363 2621 313 2778 377.

claims.title: The rate law: the j-th counter from the right loses 2<sup>j</sup>
claims.text: Between two right extensions, counter j (counted from the right, j = 1, 2, …) decreases by exactly 2<sup>j</sup> for every j up to some point; the counters beyond it are rebuilt. In 21 of the 74 transitions from step 8,225 to 2.5·10<sup>9</sup> all k counters pay, and then always a new counter appears at the front and x = 2<sup>k+3</sup> − 3 (61, 125, …, 8189, 16381). In the other 53 the rebuild starts at some counter; in 28 of them it is the first counter (from the right) smaller than its rate 2<sup>j</sup>, or its right neighbour; what decides it in general is not yet understood.

claims.title: Never one step from a halt
claims.text: The machine halts when B reads a 1, and B is entered only from A reading a 0 (A0 → 1RB). In the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps A reads a 0 8,918 times, always with a 0 to its right.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The rate law is measured, not proved, and the rebuilding of the counters that cannot pay is not yet written as a map. A proof would need both, and an invariant of the counters that keeps a 1 away from the right of A when A reads 0.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine keeps a list of counters on the tape, and they run at rates 2, 4, 8, 16, … like the digits of a binary counter seen from the side. This page shows the list, the rate law, and what is proved.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 80,023 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A wall and a list of counters
html: Each time the visited part of the tape grows on the right, the tape has the same shape:

((01)^5 is 01 five times.) For example at step 233,350,399: x = 2461 and the counters are 2693, 3139, 1283, 339, 5487, 1363, 2621, 313, 2778, 377. The wall (10)^x on the left grows by one cell per sweep; the counters are separated by 1 1 1.

sections.heading: Counter j drains at rate 2<sup>j</sup>
html: Next time the tape grows on the right (step 378,591,341), compare from the right end:

That is the law, seen at every right extension up to 2.5·109 steps for the counters at the right end of the list: the j-th counter from the right loses exactly 2j. From some counter on (often one too small to pay its rate) the list is rebuilt; when all pay, as here, a new counter is born and the wall reaches 2k+3 − 3. It is a binary counter laid out in space. These are measurements: the law is not proved.

sections.heading: What a halt would need
html: The machine stops only when B reads a 1, and B is entered only from A reading a 0. So a halt needs A>0 1, A on a 0 with a 1 right of it. At the right end A always meets 1 0 A>0 with blank tape beyond; in the first 3·106 steps A reads a 0 8,918 times and the next cell is always 0. A halt would need the rebuilding of the counters to produce a separator of a new shape. Open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.511). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.15).
After 109 steps the tape spans 80,023 cells (62,162 left of the start, 153 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

family: bouncer with a cascade of counters at rates 2, 4, 8, ...
summary: A bouncer on the left feeds a list of counters (01)^n separated by 1 1 1: at each new cell on the right, the j-th counter from the right loses exactly 2^j, up to a point where the list is rebuilt; when the whole list pays, a new counter is born and the wall is 2^(k+3) - 3.
